utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Teresa McHenry for the Office of the Prosecutor with my co-counsel Giuliano Turone and our case manager, Ms. Elles van Dusschoten. Thank you. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: The Defence appearances, please. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Good morning, your Honours. I am Edina Residovic, Defence Counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic. My co-counsel is my colleague, Eugene O'Sullivan, Professor from Canada. MR. OLUJIC (in interpretation): Good morning, your Honours. I am Zejnil Olujic, Defence Counsel for Mr. Zdravko Mucic. My co-counsel is Mr. Michael Greaves, attorney from United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. MR. KARABDIC (in interpretation): Good morning, your Honours. I am Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo. I am attorney for Mr. Hazim Delic. My co-counsel is Mr. Tom Moran, attorney from Houston Texas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am John Ackerman, attorney for Esad Landzo. My co-counsel is Cynthia McMurrey from the United States. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Ms. McHenry, what is the position with your witness before we call him in?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just ask to go into private session. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: With respect to the observation made by Mr. Ackerman yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I'm ready to respond and amplify the remarks I made yesterday, but I would ask that we do so in private session. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Let's do that before we call in the witness. Let's get into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. (In closed session)

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: (In open session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Ms. McHenry, before the witness comes, what is the date of this report?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: The copy of the report is undated. I believe the witness will indicate that it was at the end of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Whenever they file the report, I am sure they put on the date on which it has been compiled, or is it unusual?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I think it's unusual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I think there as an error in the transcript. I was not talking about Dayton. I was talking about the date on which it has been compiled. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Not Dayton Agreement. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Kindly remind the witness that he is still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I should like to remind you that you are still testifying under oath. No. No. I am just reminding you that you are testifying under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes, Ms. McHenry. You can continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Mr. D?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned previously that there were women in the camp. Can you tell us, please, how you know there were women at the camp, and if you know how many there were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I saw on the list -- I think there were five women. I could be almost certain, but the statements of these women I never saw, and the entire time we were there I was interested within the Commission about their status, but nobody was providing any answer. They said that Gordana Cecez had to stay there because there was information from the field that her husband was armed and hiding in the vicinity of Konjic. I don't know about the other women. There was a wife of Rajko Dordic, who was the Commander in Bradina, and I think she was there. After a period of time I think that I suggested that these women be released. If an interview with Gordana Cecez was necessary, it should be conducted and the information gained from it and I think that I even put in information into two reports suggesting the release of these women. I found this information from the files -- from those lists. I don't know when they were released. I don't know when these two women were released, and I think that they probably were released. How many were left there thereafter I also cannot say with certainty. I don't know if this Gordana still remained there. I don't know that exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did I understand you correctly that as part of the analysis and categorisation the Commission sometimes recommended certain prisoners for release and certain people recommended to be kept for further investigation or prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, when Mr. Zejnil was in the meeting with us I had a duty to put together an analysis as soon as possible, an analysis of all the data that we had gathered thus far, and I did that as soon as I could, based on the statements and other information that the Commission had available, and I compiled a report on behalf of the Commission, which contents are something like this. I'm not going to go at any length into it, but as follows. How these people, those Serbs in the area of Bradina and wider in the area of Konjic were arming themselves; where did the weapons come from; who was giving it to them; what types of weapons; when it was transported to Bradina and other locations around Konjic; how it was distributed; to whom it was distributed; and who were the persons from the Konjic area who took part in this. Perhaps this report contains -- I can't recall now -- some ten persons who were in the camp. Some of the persons in the report were not in the camp, because they had fled to the Borci Lake area before these combat operations, but from it all it could be -- and this is my feeling and the feeling of this Commission -- that criminal charges could be filed against those persons for inciting the armed rebellion pursuant to the laws of the former Yugoslavia. This is all that was incumbent upon us to decide.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if any of the prisoners that were categorised in the lowest categories, meaning the least serious categories, were released during the time you were working at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To be honest with you, I don't have information, feed-back who was released from the camp on that basis. Whatever I found out was by accident. I did not perceive any communication between the Commission and anybody else. It would be logical to release people. How many people were released I could only judge, not only myself but the Commission, by certain lists that were revised lists, so that we could see that these people had been released, but at that time another incident took place. They started off with the lower categories and I don't know on whose orders or whose decision this was, were transferred to Konjic, to the premises of the school and sports centre: I'm speaking the truth when I say that I don't know why this happened and who demand this had or requested this. I only heard about that, in fact, since Konjic town was under constant shelling and fire and attacks, that there was shelling and a number of civilians were killed and there were all kinds of horrors, but among others this school centre had been shelled because it was very exposed and ten or more of these prisoners were killed on that occasion. It was a real massacre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you indicated that when you were working, you could see from your office or the office from which you were working how the prisoners waited for you. Did you ever see any prisoners with their hands tied?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I sat in an office, because there were not many such offices where people who were constantly conducting this interview where they were working. Then when I would come in I would see that some were tied. Sometimes I would see it, but I know that, for instance, Zara Mrkajic was brought into this office with his hands tied, and this Zara Mrkajic was very important for the work and for the interviews that this Commission conducted, because, as one of the wealthier people in Bradina, he owned cafes. He organised the supply of arms and transportation of arms to Bradina, and as far as I can recall, this prisoner was brought in by Mr. Hazim Delic and -- you see, a person has to be prepared. He has to be made relaxed so he could talk, so that he could be clear when he talks. This could be seen. I joined in this conversation, this interview, and so we reacted. We said: "Why is he being tied?" , and very insolently he said it's none of our business. First a colleague said this. So it was a bit insulting but that's not important really. He would not untie him. We did it subsequently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it a loose tie or a tight tie, or can you please just tell us what, if anything, you observed about the manner or the effect that the hands being tied had on Mr. Mrkajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a rope. You could see that the blood circulation had been interrupted by this rope. Afterwards his hands shook and he moved them -- his hands about for the blood to start circulating normally again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after this conversation that you had with Mr. Delic about the prisoner's hands being tied?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that I can't say that I saw other people tied, with hands tied. Maybe there were others, but I personally did not observe them. Mrkajic was brought in again, another time, and that time his hands were not tied, but while we were -- while we told Zara Mrkajic to sit down on a chair -- I don't know -- I think Mr. Delic was saying things to him. I can't remember exactly what he was saying. Even though Commission members were there and he had other duties, but still he was saying these things to him. I don't know why. I had my back turned towards the door and I was looking towards the window. That was how we were sitting, and I suddenly heard a shot. Now what is that? So I was shocked, I was startled. When I turned around I think the door was open and I saw Hazim. I didn't see him fire the shot, though he always carried a rifle that was on the ready, but I didn't dare ask him, to tell you the truth, but I drew the conclusion that it was him. Sorry. I don't know what the purpose of this was, if it was him or somebody else, and I can't assert that with any certainty, but whoever did it, the aim must have been intimidation, to intimidate us, and we know that the prisoners were intimidated as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object to this because it calls for all kinds of speculation. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I think it's fairer you do not interrupt free-flowing evidence. At the end you will see where it's going. It's easier to know what is intended.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell me, the shot that was fired, could you tell if it was inside the building, if it was close to the room where you were in or if it was outside the camp, or were you able to ascertain anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in the corridor of the building in which we were working, and I wish to respond to Defence Counsel that these are not insinuations under any circumstances. I have no reason, because I don't know any of them except Mr. Delalic, with whom I went to school, so that I have no need to make any insinuations. Dear gentlemen, your Honours, I did not come to falsely testify. If I may make this small digression, I have plenty of patience. I feel honoured to report to this honourable Tribunal about all the things that were happening there and the suffering that went on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Besides what you have already testified, did you ever see anything or receive any information from anyone working in the camp indicating that prisoners were being mistreated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you see, I heard many conversations among the members of the Commission. I accepted this job in order to accomplish it honourably. Whatever I was told by Mr. Zejnil Delalic or somebody else, possibly one of the people who was in command, to do something with honour, I would do it, but hearing stories about the mistreatment of prisoners, I started thinking how I could resist, because I saw that we didn't have a Commission leader to whom we could complain. Then I saw something else. One morning when we had started working already -- I can't remember the date, because this wasn't a very long period of time that was involved. There were several men from among the Commission members who were walking around waiting for somebody to be brought in to be interviewed. In the meantime there was some kind of a panic. I didn't know what was happening. I went out into the corridor. I saw people gathering, bringing something then and then I asked "what is it". I can't remember who it was, which member of the Commission, was it Rizvic or Sacir Pajic. I don't know. He said that one of the prisoners had been beaten up and I think in the neighbouring room where we dined -- they dined, he had been brought in. I went back to the office where I was working and there were several more of us there, and we thought that we needed to check which of the prisoners it was, who had done it and why they had done it. In the meantime somebody said -- one could feel that there was an attempt to cover this whole thing up and while we were talking about this a car drove up -- I think it was a jeep -- with a driver and Mr. Delalic was there. They passed in front of the window where we were. They parked the vehicle and they entered the building. We went to see that prisoner. We entered the room and I saw that the man was in a very bad condition. He was just moaning. He was in a crouching position and some people were there whom I didn't know, probably the guards. In the meantime a doctor appeared. Who had called him, Delic or Mr. Mucic or somebody else, I don't know. So I went out. The doctor examined him and later I learned that he had been transferred to the hospital, that he had severe injuries of the lung and that his life was at risk. Where Mr. Delalic went at that moment I don't know, which room he entered. I would have liked to have met him, because I could have asked him what had happened. I was free to ask him, but I don't know where he went.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the first or the last or the nickname of this prisoner who had been reportedly beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't finish the answer to your first question. I was going to say that. I asked what his name was. Nobody seemed to know. "Is he on the list? Where does he come from?" Nobody seemed to know. Only then the people in the Commission checked and said that it was Zeljko Klimenta, known as Keljo, that he was a man from Konjic, that he had a cafe there near the petrol station at the entrance to Konjic, and nothing else: why he had been captured, why he had been brought in I did not learn.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you indicated that on this day you did not have the opportunity to talk with Mr. Delalic. During the time that you were working at Celebici did you ever attempt to contact Mr. Delalic either personally or over the telephone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, I remember telephoning. Twice I asked and I was given his number and I called Mr. Zejnil twice and on both occasions a woman answered and said that the Commander was in the field. I just introduced myself. I said who I was and what I was and my intention was to convey some things to him, things I knew, but as I didn't succeed then, why I didn't insist and try more often, I wish to explain. Listening to these stories about the mistreatment of prisoners, one morning or rather on more than one occasion I was met by a typist. I think her name was Ismeta Posder. I am not quite sure about the surname. A skinny woman. She was from Celebici by birth. Maybe she lived there too. As the weather was fine, it was summer time, and I would come quite early to work and she would offer me a cup of coffee, and she was making coffee anyway for us. She complained to me then that they were mistreating prisoners at night, that women were being raped. I was shocked, and when she said that the guards had boasted of having raped somebody last night -- you see, they had raped this Gorza woman, Gordana Cecez and some others, and she was horrified, having heard of these cases. I said to her: "We should tell this to Mr. Delalic" and she said that she knew Delalic and that she would convey this to him. In this connection she referred most often to Mr. Delic. Maybe she knew him from before or better than me, but without specifying exactly what he had done and what other guards may have done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you know if any prisoners died at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know in which buildings those prisoners were and where they had been brought from, but one day I noticed that there were several prisoners in a building just in front of the building where we were working. I think it must have been a break. We were having lunch or something. I can't remember. Anyway, I was in front of the building and some other members of the Commission. Somebody said that the father of Zarko Mrkajic had died in that building. His name did figure on the list but I didn't know that it was his father. I could see from the data on the list that he was an old man. Somebody had opened the door of that building. They were going in and coming out, and I saw somebody kneeling next to him, but I didn't enter. I saw this from afar. Afterwards they told me that it was his other son. So I think I found him on that list too, because there are a lot of people of the same surname, Mrkajic, so you couldn't link them all together, the relationships among them. Logically the Commission should have, with the assistance of a doctor and other experts, established the cause of death, but the Commission was informed by someone that this Mrkajic had died of natural causes, that he suffered from diabetes. He probably didn't receive medicine or something else. I suppose I can assume that, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the normal procedure, whether or not -- what the procedure was if a prisoner died, if there was a medical certificate, or investigations? Do you know how that worked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You have put to me a very good question, a question that we kept asking ourselves when we were there. "What are we to do if a prisoner dies of natural or non-natural causes?" People would wink at one another and say: "Don't ask such a question". To tell you the truth, I was horrified, and then I said: "Can we fight against evil by resorting to the same kind of evil? No". Then in the Commission again I said that if we learned of somebody's death we would have to -- we need to find out about the death certificate and that sort of thing, and nobody knew the answers. Then it was not just me but all the other members of the Commission could see this lady. Her name was Jasna Dzumhur. When we saw her in the corridor of the building, of course we said "Hello", as we knew each other. It was wartime. We enquired about family members and so on, which was quite normal. Then I asked her what she was doing there, assuming she knew what I was doing in the Commission. She said that she had come to take over a corpse. Then I said: "Well, Mrs. Jasna, how come the Commission knows nothing about it?" She said: "Why should you know anyway?" She was angry and she just marched off. I hadn't insulted her in any way. "Why don't you kill them?", she said. I conveyed this to the Commission and all the Commission members just shrugged their shoulders. Who had died on that occasion? What kind of certificate had been given? Who had established the causes of death? That was absolutely unknown to me and the Commission members; at least I didn't hear anything from the Commission members, and I know that everyone was astounded. Maybe she came more often. I saw her car sometimes but I didn't see her in person, but they said that she had the authority to take over or to take care of the people who died or who had been killed. I don't know what the name of this position she held was, but later I met her on several occasions, when I had abandoned the Commission, almost every other day when I continued my duties in the military police, and we would exchange a few words often. Afterwards I referred to this and her answer always was that she had informed Mr. Delalic about everything. I do not know whether that was so. It was not up to me to verify this, but I said that that was not correct, and that the Prosecution should be established to do its work properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned -- may I ask you whether or not with respect to any particular detainees, whether or not in addition to any analytical work that may have been done, did you ever have any conversations with anyone in the camp concerning why a particular detainee was being kept in the camp or something like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, I had already decided that I had to do something, because I cannot continue this battle that I was waging with my very self to watch these people and to wait for somebody to kill me or not to let me have lunch, as Mr. Hazim Delic wouldn't allow me when it was Bajram, because he told me that I couldn't eat. Probably according to his criteria I hadn't deserved it and thank God that I didn't meet his criteria, though it was an honour for me to sit with my colleagues on the occasion of Bajram. Towards the end, when I had already decided to abandon this job, I think it was Stenek or somebody else who was there too, and he said to me: "Look, will you please have an interview with this man", an elderly man from Konjic. "We feel embarrassed. We know him and he's done nothing". I said: "If you feel awkward about it, I don't know the man. Why shouldn't I do it?" So I went into a neighbouring office. I asked the man his name. I remember he said Stanojevic Vladimir. Stanojevic, I think that was his name. He was an elderly man. We sat down and he talked, why he had been brought in, when. Judging by all he told me there was absolutely no reason. He had a pistol with a permit of the authorities in those days. He had surrendered it voluntarily. That is what he said. He even said that he had a receipt. He was a Serb by nationality. He said that his house had been searched several times afterwards. Then I went to the Commission and told them there was no reason to detain this person in this camp, and the people shrugged their shoulders and said: "We don't know". Though this was not my duty, I went to Mr. Mucic and I asked him: "Do you have any official record or report as to why this man was brought in?" Mr. Mucic must remember this. He said there was nothing. "Well, how are we going to keep him? He should be released. Why is he here?" He didn't say anything. Of course, I went out. I left his office. I went back. I continued my work, saying that there was no need to continue interviewing this man. The next day they said that I had to take a statement from him, that everyone has to make a statement. Whoever is captured has to make some kind of a statement. So I said: "All right. There's no problem. I'll take a statement". The man was brought in. I spoke to him. A typist typed out this report regarding the pistol. I even remember that he said his son-in-law was an officer of the former JNA and that he had stayed in the region of Krajina and he linked this to his own case, thinking that was maybe the reason why he had been captured, but as telephone and other communications had been interrupted, it had nothing to do -- he had no communication with his son-in-law. He didn't even though whether he was alive or dead. I put this down. Then again I went to speak to Mr. Mucic on my own initiative and I asked him, and then he replied with a certain amount of arrogance, and I said that: "Why do we have to detain me (sic)?" He said: "He was a Serb and he was a personnel man in the firm of Igman". I didn't know that but I did know he was a Serb. Still I didn't see any reason why and I don't know when he was released. I think that we left in the meantime. Then there was another one. This man can confirm the details if he's alive. There was another case of a Professor, a teacher of philosophy or something like that, or maybe political sciences, from the village of Idbar. I think he wore a beard. He was a youngish man. He was brought in. We didn't see any reasons in writing, nor were any oral reasons conveyed to us. I know the man said that he had left his parents in the village of Idbar, that he had not been a member of any military formations. I don't know when he was released or whether he was released, but those are the two cases I can remember. I can't recall his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, as time went on, you have indicated that you became more concerned about what was happening in Celebici. What, if anything, did you and any other members of the Commission ultimately do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I myself and others, too, were very -- very bitterly complained and said what should be done. We all realised that this was just a facade, this whole Commission, which was supposed to sort of provide some semblance of lawfulness to all this, but it was, in fact, nothing. People had no answer to this. Let me correct myself. Yesterday I said that we also may have worked Saturdays. No, we did not. On Saturday -- one Saturday, because we didn't work, I went looking for Mr. Ivica Azinovic at the HVO, even though, truth be told, that was not simple to go and say that you refused to go and do this job, because I did describe how I started this job. I had decided not to refuse any work that would be in the interest of the defence of the people and of peace. On that Saturday I didn't know what to expect, whether it would be accepted or not. I didn't know what information they may possess. I waited in front of the HVO. It was almost the early afternoon. He never showed up and they never told me where Azinovic was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Mr. Azinovic's role, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was the President of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please continue, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That evening I went to where I lived at that time, but the next morning, on Sunday, I came back. I knew that these institutions were working because of the situation. So I waited for him on Sunday, because I was told that he was coming. Around noon Azinovic showed up and I waited and then he invited me into the office. I came into the office and told him everything I knew, which I am now telling you, your Honours, what was going on in the prison, in this camp, and that I could not listen and watch these things, and least of all do the job that I was assigned to do. As far as I could see, he was surprised and he said that he had no information of that kind. I told him, of course, that it wasn't my duty to come and pass this information to him, but since I've told him this, I told him that I could not continue to work on this any more. I don't know whether he believed me or not, but he said that he had to talk to the other members of the Commission that day, that he had to talk -- may I say this in private session in continuation of this question?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask that we go into private session. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes. It is only one type of evidence, but let's go into it. (In closed session).

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: (In open session)

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, we are now in public session. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (No translation).

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, I am going to ask that you hold on because we are having some problems with interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then the three of us waited and then they called other people. There was Dinko Zebic. I didn't know him at that time. I only met him later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Mr. Dinko Zebic's position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he was the military commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of what unit or what entity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The military units of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were some other members of the HVO and then again I said what I had told him privately, and the other two who were present there confirmed this, and further elaborated with additional details, which I did not know. Azinovic said only one thing: "If this is the situation, you must leave there and not work there any more". I said: "Yes, I accept that. I agree with that", but I proposed not to just leave there, because it is not just us who are members of the Commission. There are four additional members of this Commission who also respond in the same way. Then he said: "So what are you suggesting?" I said: "I'm suggesting that we put it down in writing, the reasons for which we do not wish to continue working there", and I vouched that all members of the Commission are going to sign this. The next day -- this was a Monday -- they agreed to this, the people at the HVO, Azinovic and the rest, and this report was drawn -- drafted. We did not say that it had to be done the very next day, but the next day -- I remember it was a Monday -- this report was drafted. That Monday I had already planned before some other business that I had to tend to, so I did not get there in time. I think I arrived in Celebici on Tuesday and I didn't find any members of the Commission there. Then I realised that what we had agreed on was done and I went to the HVO to report there. I think I found there...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness mentioned a name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: ... and other members of the Commission, and we talked about all the irregularities we had observed, that the Commander of the TO, the President of the HVO, the co-ordinator of the combat operations, the tactical group, which is the post that Mr. Delalic occupied, and that there was a copy of this in the archives of the HVO. I saw this. I picked up the copy to see whether everything that we had mentioned, all the irregularities had been recorded. Then I said I agreed about all the details. However, had I been present at the drafting there, I would have been more specific. I would have added more details and I would not have wanted to see just those general things that were stated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. Let me go back and make sure that everything was understood correctly. Am I correct that when you came back to Celebici and found no-one there you then went to the HVO headquarters and learned that the report had been written; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mentioned the names -- do you know. You mentioned some names, but can I just clarify: to whom was this report sent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The report was sent -- this is what we had agreed and this is what was said, who would be informed: the Commander of the Territorial Defence in Konjic, the TO Commander; the President of the HVO in Konjic; the co-ordinator of the combat operations, Sarajevo district. I don't know what area this comprised of. That was Mr. Delalic. The TO Commander, I think it was Ramic. The President of the HVO was Ivica Azinovic. I don't know if it was sent to anyone else. I cannot recall that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. With the usher's assistance ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I ask for some patience that I am able to read this through? (Pause). Yes, this is the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe, sir, what you have been shown has been marked for identification purposes as Prosecution Exhibit 162. Sir, did I understand you correctly that this is a copy of the report that you were just testifying about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is a copy of that report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. At the time that you went and got the copy from the archives, did you review it and was it -- can you just tell me whether the things mentioned in the report were accurate and either observed by you or told to you by one of the other Commission members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some -- a part of it is what the members of the Commission saw and told and some I observed myself, and when I took it from the archives I read it and I signed it. I was one of the last to put a signature on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I correct, sir, that in terms of the official report, it had already been signed and forwarded before you had an opportunity to sign it, because you were out of town; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, and some other members, I think, were not there at the time, but the report was forwarded to that, and I later verified that this report had been forwarded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. How can you verify that, in fact, the report had been forwarded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, I verified this in the HVO. I did not verify it either at the TO or with Delalic directly, but in contact with other people, for instance, Mrs. Jasna was either a member of the War Presidency or something, and when we would meet, among other things, she would mention the issue of resolving the problems about the camp, and this was not my problem any more, but on a private basis I warned her. I said: "You have international institutions present here on the territory of Konjic. There's the Red Cross, other humanitarian organisations. Something needs to be done. Is this something that can go on in a civilised society, that in this defence that we -- that blemishes the defence and the position that we found ourselves in?" While I was in this Investigative Commission we tried to do something, but we could not do something, so we wrote the report. You have to clear the matters in this camp". I objected to her taking over these dead bodies without authorisation. I don't know how she got authorisation to do that. She told me that she informed commander Zejnil of everything. My assumption is that she knew. She didn't ask: "Why did you write this report?", but my understanding was it is obvious that she knew about this. She must have been informed. Then, further, I felt sorry for these people for what was done, and a lot were not involved. These people were left at the mercy, but later, as I continued working in Konjic, everybody knew that something ugly was going on there, that the Commission was not going there, so these were rumours going around. I think that I had already left. I don't know what period this was. Mr. Zejnil can remember this. I was sitting in a cafe near the gas station in Konjic. There were a lot of people that I knew from Konjic, especially from the MUP. I complained to these people from the MUP, that is I asked -- I was asking for help in a sense that if somebody manages to get from Sarajevo, which was under siege, to come to Konjic, to check for me whether a relative of mine, who was a member of the Ministry of the Interior at Sarajevo, whether he was alive or not. One of the members of the MUP told me, when I enquired about this -- he said: "Bakir Alispahic came. He is in Konjic. If you see him, look him up. He is with Zejnil. Ask him to check this for you". I asked these people who knew Bakir whether they saw him. This was now towards the evening, and he -- I was told that he went to Orahovica with Zejnil. Now Orahovica may be just a few hundred metres from Konjic. They pointed to the house. It was just off the main road. I sat in my car and went to this house. Indeed, I found Mr. Zejnil there with another group of people -- I don't know -- his friends or his business partners. He introduced me to some of them -- in fact, to all of them. He would introduce some of them to me. He said: "This man is from Sarajevo Television". Some of these faces I knew from public -- as public personalities. I told him why I came to see him. He apologised. He said he didn't have time to sit down with me but if I had anything, to give him -- to do so. I wrote down a message for Bakir to check for me whether this person was alive and Zejnil took it and said he would pass it on to this person and if he found out anything, that this person would pass it on back to Zejnil. He'll tell me. At that time -- in fact, this was the only time that I met with Zejnil Delalic. He never asked me about the report: "Why did you write it?", whether it was true or not. Had he thought that it was necessary for us to talk about it -- I don't know if he considered it necessary to talk about it, but if it was the talk of the town, as they say in our parts, then maybe he could have discussed this with me. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, after the report, did you work any more in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I absolutely stopped working there. The moment I was told that I should put some distance between myself and this, and I needed this kind of approval, because I couldn't just leave on my own. It would have even been risky to have just left. That would be sort of dereliction of duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I move into evidence Prosecution Exhibit 162 and that will conclude my examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You have not sorted out the date of this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: You are right. I am sorry, your Honour. When was it that this report was written and forwarded to the addressees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, that's a mistake. That is really a mistake. That's an omission that the date was not written, but this was between 20th and 30th June. Now I don't know where exactly in that period this was, but really this was a mistake, that the date was not put down.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, at this time I move 162 into evidence and I have no questions -- additional questions. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: The Defence has seen it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, your Honour. The Defence received this months ago. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: It is admitted in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, as I said, this finishes our examination-in-chief. It may be that, like the last witness, there will be no cross-examination, but if for some reason there is some cross-examination, I would just, with your Honours' permission, like to remind Defence Counsel that this witness is particularly sensitive, and so if there's any doubt about a question, the Prosecution at least would request that we go into private session. Thank you. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: It is 11.30 now. We will break and come back at 12.00 for possible cross-examination. (11.30 am) (Short break) (12.00) JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Have you now decided the order of cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, we have, your Honour. We will proceed in this way: first, counsel for Mr. Delalic; second, counsel for Mr. Mucic; third, counsel for Mr. Delic; and, last, counsel for Mr. Landzo. Thank you. Cross-examination by Ms. Residovic MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): I beg your indulgence, your Honours, until I organise myself. May it please the court? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes, you can take the witness. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you. Good day, Mr. D. My name is Edina Residovic. I am Defence Counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic. Mr. D, we may know each other from before, but I am sure that, as a witness under oath --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me. We are having some motions from the booth and I don't know what it is about. I think maybe something is wrong with the headsets or something.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: The witness' microphone is not on. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Okay. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: In fact, I can see without him touching it there is a loose connection. Maybe there is an intermittent fault which ought to be cured before we go further. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Kindly check them. Look at it. Make sure it doesn't go off again. Yes, you can continue. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you. Mr. D, our greetings were not heard, because of your microphone, but I think we understood one another. Good day, Mr. D.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know that I am Defence Counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that you are the Defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. D, I would not like to warn you, but to draw your attention to a fact of which you may not be conscious, and it is something that I too often forget. It is very important that what we are saying should be heard by the Trial Chamber and all others here present in this courtroom, and since we speak a language that we understand, we tend to put questions and answer them at great speed. So I would like to ask you, when you hear my question, to wait for the interpretation by our interpreters and I, too, will do my best to wait while I hear the interpretation of what you have said. This will slow down our conversation but I think it would be more useful for all round. Have we understood one another?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We have quite, madam attorney.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Since I will be asking certain questions which might indicate the identity of the witness, I would request that we go into private session. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: We can go into private session. I think we might keep it so throughout the cross-examination. (In closed session)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (In open session) MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Mr. D, before going on to the next group of questions, I should like to ask you to confirm whether I understood well your answer to a question from the Prosecution that you had worked in the military investigating commission for about one month; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I cannot remember whether it was less. It's more probably less, but roughly that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you left for Konjic from the Mostar HVO, you were given a letter and a permit indicating that you should report to the Konjic HVO; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Actually there was no other way for you to leave Mostar, because the regulations of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna at that time required that all military conscripts had to have permission to leave their place of residence. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because it was impossible to pass through the checkpoint without that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you reached Konjic, you reported to the Konjic HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, Mr. D, in view of the time that has elapsed since those events, let us repeat and try to specify the time that you have indicated in your testimony in the Trial Chamber. Is it true that on that day you first dropped in the place of Ostrozac, which for those who do not know is a place called Ostrozac south of Konjic and Celebici towards Mostar, and which belongs to the municipality of Jablanica. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what I said and explained. May I clarify a little, if I may, briefly?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very briefly. You have answered my question, but I can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, from Ostrozac you have to go across a hanging bridge to Butrovic Polje and that is where I was going. If you are interested, I can tell you whose greetings I was conveying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That will not be necessary. Thank you. You explained that that was the day when combat operations in Bradina ended and you explained why you remember that particular day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe that's what I said, but there were groups of soldiers coming back and there was firing, and without knowing what was happening, I asked what it was, and they said there had been combat operations in the territory of Bradina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, Mr. D, if the battles in Bradina ended on 27th or 28th May, then you reached Ostrozac roughly on that date; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From Ostrozac, Mr. D, you went on to your family house in Butrovic Polje, and the following day you went to Konjic and reported to the HVO. Did I understand your testimony well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, your first arrival in Konjic could have been somewhere around 28th May or 29th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember the date, but I said the end of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct and can you confirm that two or three days after that and after all the discussions you had in the HVO, you tried to go back to Mostar, but because of the shelling of the road we have referred to, you were unable to enter Mostar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Was that the same day I was -- after having reported to the HVO I said I would go to Mostar, and I went back. That may have been the same day. I can't tell each individual day. It could have been that very same day or the next day. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, if, Mr. D, you testified in this courtroom that after the talk you had in the HVO you headed for Mostar two or three days later and then came back again, because you couldn't enter due to shelling, that is not absolutely true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those were the days I was in the HVO, but so much time has gone by since I can't remember what day it was, but it is true that I went there and I came back, because I had to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. D, didn't you testify that after coming back from Mostar, or rather after failing to enter Mostar, you reported the next day again to the HVO, and came across somebody called Zovko, who told you that you should report to Goran Lokas? Is that right? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was the same day I was coming from Mostar and I continued to Konjic and reported to the HVO immediately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, Mr. D, if you said in your testimony and your previous statement that you did that the following day, then that is not quite correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whether that was the next day or not, I told you that I went to Mostar. I couldn't enter. I came back and went on to Konjic, and told the HVO I couldn't enter Mostar. "If you have any duties for me, I can work here too. There'll be no problems".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just wanted to check that if you said -- asserted that you had done this the next day, you are now saying that you are not quite sure of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't say with precision that it was the next day, but I know where I went and why I went, but the exact time, I don't think there's any dispute between us. It's normal for you to ask me these things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. D: I know that you are a witness who has come here to tell the truth and who is speaking under oath, and I know my duties too, so will you please tell me, is it true that you also stated before this Trial Chamber that on that day you didn't find Goran Lokas, because you learned that he had had an accident, and according to your testimony this could have been somewhere around 1st or 2nd June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't say that it was 1st or 2nd June. . Your Honour, I know to came to Konjic to the HVO. Whether those combat operations were still going on in Bradina or not, I wasn't informed about that at all, and how long those operations lasted I didn't know at the time. I didn't know. The day when I found Zovko, whether it was Zovko or somebody else, and when he said that Lokas was not there ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you didn't find Goran Lokas, Mr. D, you went back to Butrovic Polje, and the following day from your sister-in-law you learned that Miroslav Stenek had been looking for you and that he had left a message that you should report to the HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I received that message. Stenek may have looked for me that same day that I was looking for Lokas. I don't know. I can't tell for sure, because we didn't see one another, but anyway, when I returned from Konjic I got this message, because it's not so easy to pass on the message. Whether he had looked for me that day or the day before, I can't tell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, Mr. D, the next day, after you went looking for Mr. Lokas, you found out from your sister-in-law that you were looked for by Mr. Miroslav Stenek?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, after I had gone over to them she said he was coming but when he was coming I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. D, you claim that you visited your sister-in-law on the day when you were returning from Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I think I even went -- well, on both sides, when going there and when coming back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. D, if yesterday before this Trial Chamber you testified that the next day, the day after you were informed -- when you were asked to look for Goran Lokas, you found out from your sister-in-law that Miro Stenek was looking for you, then what you testified to yesterday is not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One thing is correct. I cannot really differentiate these days. All this took place within a day or two, and I cannot say now. Maybe I would have to be especially reminded. In fact, I wasn't even interested in these things. I reported to where I was told to report. Whether this was a couple of days before the 1st or it was on the 1st, but this is how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. D, you now claim that all this happened within a day or two in the period of when you first arrived in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe it was even three.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. D, if yesterday during questioning by the Prosecution you testified before this Trial Chamber that certain things happened within two or three days or the next day, and you said that all this lasted eight or nine days, then what you said was not entirely true; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I apologise. I don't know what I said that took eight or nine days, what was happening over a period of eight or nine days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In order for you to better understand my questions, you said that you came to Konjic, that this was the day when the fighting in Bradina stopped, which was 27th May. Then you said that on the next day you went to the HVO in Konjic. That would be then 29th May. Then before this Trial Chamber you said that within two or three days you went to and tried to go back to Mostar. That would be an additional two or three days. Then you testified that you came back and the next day you went to try to establish contact with Zovko, whose first name you didn't know. That would be another day, day number five. Then you testified that you tried to find Goran Lokas and you couldn't find him, but then -- and then you testified that your sister-in-law the next day told you that Miro Stenek was looking for you, and then you testified that the day after that, after this information, you again went to the HVO. That would make a total of eight to nine days, Mr. D. If this is what you stated, Mr. D, then you did not tell the truth before this Trial Chamber; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour. She can ask him if he made a mistake. She can ask him to clarify. She can ask him if there was some confusion, but to say whether or not he told the truth, given that he has already explained what happened, I think is unfair to the witness. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Mr. D, are there big discrepancies between what you have testified to before this Trial Chamber and what you are saying now, that all this only took two or three days? My question is: do you see a big difference between these two statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is not the kind of analysis that I made, but I said in brief when I arrived in Ostrozac I was told that the shooting was all coming from soldiers who were in Bradina involved in the combat operations. You are mentioning the 27th. 27th May means nothing to me. It was confusion in those days. I can only speak to the days which are in some documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. D, I would just like to go back to the questions I would ask of you. Could you say not the dates, but the period of two or three days and of eight or nine days are two different periods? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I thought you had made your own observation of the effect of that. Go on to other questions. You made your own evaluation on that. He might be lying. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you, your Honours. Mr. D, you met at the HVO with a person named Zovko, whom at that time you did not know. Did you later find out who this person Zovko was? Was this Zvonko Zovko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was not Zvonko Zovko. I said that I was not sure that his name was Zovko. He was blond, medium height, in his 40s. I also saw him later, but I cannot recall the name now. I mentioned him. Maybe the President of the HVO was not around so I was received in his office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. D, you reported to the HVO and, as you said, you there stated that if you were not able to go back to Mostar that you were prepared to take on some duties in Konjic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that I was at their disposal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the same day you did not go to the MUP, the service from which you retired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that day, Mr. D, you didn't go either to the -- you also did not go to the Territorial Defence headquarters in Konjic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were aware that at that time, pursuant to regulations of Bosnia and Herzegovina concerning mobilisation, the HVO was the organisation that would appoint members of the Croatian community to such duties and posts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were referred to Mr. Goran Lokas at the HVO in Konjic, you knew at that time that he was in charge of the security affairs at the HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I did not know that he was in charge of the security affairs. I was told that Goran Lokas works for -- in the military investigative commission. I didn't know -- I didn't ask what this Commission was, where it was working, what the duties were, but from the name itself I understood that it was a commission that dealt with military affairs in connection with this war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. D, it was not strange to you that Mr. Miroslav Stenek was looking for you at your sister-in-law's, because you, in fact, knew Mr. Miroslav Stenek personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right. I don't know why it should have been strange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Miroslav Stenek was also an official with the Ministry of Internal Affairs, just like you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You knew in the same way Goran Lokas, who worked in the internal -- Ministry for the Interior at the same time as you did and then later became a judge with the court for misdemeanours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that he was first the judge with the court for misdemeanours and then was the secretary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. D, you said that just in front of the HVO -- in the hallway you met Mr. Azinovic, whom you had not known before, and who had just arrived with his driver?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also stated that immediately you went with him to Mr. Delalic's house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also stated that you personally know Mr. Delalic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You not only went to the same school with him, but in the same classroom; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you entered Mr. Delalic's apartment, this was the only person in the apartment whom you knew personally; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only person I knew at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for that reason it seemed obvious to you that he would be the only one to greet you and then introduce you to other persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you already knew the name of Mr. Ivica Azinovic, can you also tell us what other persons were present in Mr. Delalic's apartment and whose names you learned after you were introduced to them after Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only -- I shook hands with this man, but only later did I find out that Dinko Zebic -- until that time I had never seen the man or known him, or knew about what his position was either in the HVO or any other place, and I wasn't even interested in that, but the two of them -- in fact, Mr. Zejnil had some papers in his hand, some kind of chart or some kind of a sketch drawn by hand, and the same thing also had Dinko Zebic in his hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dinko Zebic wore a military uniform; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall. There were men in uniforms there and some who did not have uniforms. I cannot recall, but it is possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time Mr. Delalic introduced Dinko Zebic, the head of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Mr. Zejnil Delalic did not introduce me to any people in particular. There are several of them there. I did shake hands of them, the ones who were standing up. Those who were sitting down at a small coffee table I did not. As we were standing and shaking hands he was introducing me but he wasn't introducing anybody back to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. D, this is the first time that you saw Mr. Dinko Zebic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the first time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, Mr. D, if today during your testimony and when asked by the Prosecutor you claim that you saw Dinko Zebic for the first time when you came to describe the conditions in Celebici, together with your colleagues from the Commission, with your colleague Zovko, that would not be true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is not what I said. It was that -- that it was on that occasion that I met Dinko Zebic, because on that occasion, when I met him in the room with Mr. Zejnil Delalic, I also met him in passing several times, and I obviously asked who the Commander of the HVO was, and I found out. So I'm sorry. I did not state that. It is either a mistake in interpreting or you heard-mistakenly, but until that time I had never been with him, that is true, nor had I any need to be with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at the time when you visited Mr. Delalic's house you had no personal knowledge about what Mr. Delalic was doing or what his duties and what his authorities were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until that moment absolutely no information. I could make assumptions, but nobody told me, but inferences --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I wasn't really asking you about inferences, only what you knew. Mr. D, you said that the next day you joined in the work of the military investigative commission in Celebici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if -- how you explained your -- the process by which you arrived at working in this Commission, that could have taken place only on 3rd or 4th June, but since you've clarified this, I'm just pointing to the discrepancy which showed up in your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really cannot speak to the dates precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is why I'm not asking you that. Several days after the start of your work is it true that a meeting took place with Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you be more precise, since this is a short period of time, the period of time that you worked in this Commission, about 30 days? How many days could it have been from the day when you started working for the Commission and the day which took place, as you said, where Mr. Delalic was also present? Could you be more precise about what this "several days" means? Is it two, three, four?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I were able to talk about dates, I would gladly do so. Two days, three days. I say short period of time, and I didn't say that I worked for 30 days. I never stated an exact number of days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise. I month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't even say a month. I said up to a month, and it is possible that this was 20 plus days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise if I misquote you some time, but it has all been taken down in transcript very precisely, so there's no controversy there. So my question to you is: the day you went to work in this Commission up until the day when this meeting took place, could you tell us, at least approximately, how many days would that be? More than two days and less than seven days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really cannot even talk about that within that framework. I only know that several days went by.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that before this Trial Chamber you testified that after this meeting Mr. Delalic gave you a piece of paper, as you said, sort of a certificate for you to be able to -- a permit for you to be able to leave Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I misspoke, what -- I can't recall now, but at first I asked for this piece of paper so that I would be able to go to Mostar, because I was not able to do that, but if I said that, I misspoke, if I said that this happened then, in this meeting. I know that I asked him and I told him that I had to go. Now how this happened that he wrote this for me, whether I asked through somebody else and then he had it delivered to me, to be honest, it didn't matter to me. I just needed this permit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. D, when asked very precisely by the Prosecutor whether on that day you also had a personal piece of business that you did with Mr. Delalic, you then said that Mr. Delalic gave you this permit, which you identified before all of us. Is it correct that this is how you had stated it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Until this meeting, until this meeting took place, I had not gone. I was talking about my need to go, and when I asked this permit, I told him -- I said: "I don't know when I will go". Then indeed, as a colleague and a gentleman, he said: "Fine", and gave it to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the day when you talked, is it on that day that he gave you this permit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I said that it was then, then it was my mistake. I misspoke. He didn't give me that piece of paper then, but at that time we did discuss my departure. We talked about it. I should have gone. Maybe I said -- I may have heard the news that the shelling was very bad and I couldn't go, but there was discussion of that -- about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When asked by me and before that, before this Trial Chamber, that the HVO issued permits for the militarily able persons to leave the city; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You knew that Mr. Delalic had no duty with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time -- I don't know. At that time I didn't know anything. I only saw Mr. Delalic in some kind of command position when I got there. I didn't know anything else and I wasn't interested in anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. D, to go back to your joining the Commission, on the day when you were in Mr. Delalic's house with Mr. Azinovic, between then and the meeting you held, you never saw Mr. Delalic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that I even signed up on a uniform in Mr. Delalic's house, but whether this was before the meeting or after the meeting I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Mr. D, Mr. Delalic had authority to issue you a uniform; is that correct? You noticed that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know if he had authority, but the first time -- the first day when I talked to him, I told him that I would need a uniform, and I think that at that time he said that there was no problem for me to come and pick up a uniform, and somebody issued this uniform to me, and I signed off on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I saw you look up. I thought you were watching the clock. The Trial Chamber will go into a break. We will come back at 2.30. (1.00 pm) (Luncheon adjournment) 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25 (2.30 pm) JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: We can continue, Ms. Residovic. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you, your Honours. Mr. D, I should like to go back a little bit to discuss the meeting which you said was held on June 1st and which was attended by Mr. Delalic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (No translation) I did not say it was held on June 1st.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. D, on page 5180 of the English text you were shown a document. Before I go on to that question, I should like to ask you whether you can confirm what is stated in the transcript on page 5180, namely that on that day at a meeting of the Commission -- the meeting of the Commission was attended, as stated in lines 13-18, which members of the Commission, (redacted) (redacted) --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: May I just ask that the members of the Commission not all be said in public session? MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, I propose we have a private session until the end of my cross-examination, because I don't know which of the names I am mentioning may be protected witnesses and I think this would facilitate the proceedings for all of us. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Thank you very much. I think it's a surer way of allowing you to cross-examine without difficulty. So let's all go into private session. I suppose we will not have these problems again. Thank you. (In closed session)

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Court adjourned at 5.30 pm until the following morning 10.00 am

procedural_notes.text: Pages 5267 to 5330 redacted in closed session
